background.definition: Epileptic seizures are sudden, transient behavioral alterations caused by abnormal, excessive neuronal activity in the cerebral cortex. Epilepsy is diagnosed when 2 or more unprovoked seizures occur on separate days.

list.listitem: Approximately 150,000 adults experience a first seizure annually in the United States.
Cumulative lifetime incidence for seizure occurrence is estimated at 10% and of epilepsy 3%.
Approximately 30% to 50% of incipient seizures recur and become epilepsy.
Incidence of epilepsy is 25 to 200 per 100,000 in adulthood, increasing after the age of 60 years.

A systematic review of 197 international prevalence studies concluded that the point prevalence of active epilepsy was 6.4 per 1000 persons, while the lifetime prevalence was 7.6 per 1000 persons. There was relatively little difference in prevalence by age or sex.
A typical full-time-practice generalist will encounter 5 to 10 patients with seizure disorder per year.
There is an association between seizure disorder and psychiatric disorders including anxiety (OR 2.1), depression (OR 2.5), and bipolar disorder (OR 3.0).
Epilepsies are either idiopathic, symptomatic, or cryptogenic (ie, when an underlying pathological cause is presumed but cannot be proved).
Seizures may be provoked by drug use, alcohol intoxication or withdrawal, metabolic dyscrasias such as hypoglycemia, infection, inflammation, ischemia, or trauma, or they may be unprovoked.
Aggravating influences include physical or emotional stress, sleep deprivation, and concurrent systemic illness.
Family history and remote neurologic events or chronic degenerative neurologic conditions are risk factors.
The rate of seizures was less than 0.01% (1 in 10,000) following mRNA COVID-19 vaccination. This rate is much lower than that seen with COVID-19 infection.
Seizures are either partial/focal in onset (arising from one brain region) or primary generalized (bisynchronous from onset).
Opposing brain influences of excessive neuronal hypersynchrony and/or failure of neural inhibitory drive may give rise to seizures.
Routine prophylaxis is not routinely recommended in patients with a brain malignancy. A
There is no evidence from two clinical trials with 856 subjects (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.34 - 1.26) to support prevention of seizures after stroke. C
If anticonvulsants are used postoperatively, taper them 1 week after surgery in patients who have not had a seizure. B
Patients receiving chronic antiepileptic drug therapy should be screened for reduced bone density, and women of child-bearing potential with epilepsy should receive folic acid daily. C
Prophylactic use of antiepileptic drugs reduces early seizures in patients with traumatic brain injury (NNT = 10) but there is no evidence of long-term benefit or reduction in disability or death. B

A systematic review of patients receiving seizure prophylaxis during the first 7 days following mild to moderate TBI identified 8 studies with 5637 patients. The absolute risk reduction for prevention of seizures with prophylaxis was 0.6% (NNT 160). B
Diagnosis is made by clinical history or direct observation of a seizure. C
Although the diagnosis of a seizure or epilepsy remains clinical, supportive diagnostic tests including brain MRI and EEG have significant yield and impact on prognosis for seizure recurrence. B
Most adults with new-onset seizures should receive either a brain MRI (preferred) or head CT to exclude underlying symptomatic brain pathology. C
Baseline serum labs have low diagnostic yield but may help ensure safety in initiating drug therapy. C
If seizures are atypical or a patient fails to respond to empiric antiepileptic drug therapy, consider admission for video-EEG monitoring. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Often provoked by change from recumbent to standing position, little postictal confusion
Usually without loss of consciousness, more often with neurological deficit (paralysis, hypesthesia)
Presence of headache usual, often long sensory march (symptoms progress over several minutes)
Usually accompanied by other symptoms of primary sleep disorder
Eyes closed rather than open, unusual movements, explosive onset, often prolonged
No loss of consciousness; involuntary, relatively stereotyped movements

list.listitem: A thorough clinical history of characteristic ictal (during seizure) and periictal symptoms and signs is essential for diagnosing seizures or epilepsy. Seizures are only a symptom of brain dysfunction, so a seizure is not in itself an etiologic diagnosis.
Ictal behavioral alterations are diverse, ranging from subjective auras to objectively witnessed behavioral arrest, staring, unresponsiveness, and involuntary movements.
Common although not invariable postictal symptoms include sleepiness, snoring respirations, tongue biting, self-injury, and urinary or stool incontinence.

Interictal symptoms may include mood problems, memory or cognitive disturbances, and common symptoms of toxicity such as sleepiness, dizziness, diplopia, or ataxia in patients receiving antiepileptic drugs.
Provoked seizures result from an extrinsic systemic or intrinsic brain factor. Causes of provoked seizures are listed in .

Partial seizures are classified as simple partial when consciousness is preserved, such as a subjective aura of sensory or visual symptoms, or focal motor movements. Partial complex seizures include altered consciousness and typically involve staring, unresponsiveness, and involuntary movements. EEG shows focal epileptiform activity, and MRI may be normal or demonstrate focal cortical pathology.

Generalized seizures most often involve either staring with consciousness impairment (absence), a sudden muscle jerk (myoclonic), or convulsion of the body (tonic-clonic). EEG shows generalized epileptiform activity, and CT or MRI is typically normal.

An EEG may support the clinical diagnosis of epilepsy; a sleep recording increases the yield for interictal epileptiform discharges. Abnormal EEGs are seen in 51% of adults presenting with an apparent unprovoked first seizure.

Head CT may be used in acute settings to exclude CNS pathology such as brain hemorrhage or infarction that may require emergent management. Head CT scanning is abnormal in 15% of adults presenting with an apparent first unprovoked seizure and significantly abnormal (ie, the findings affected patient management) in 10%.

The yield for a brain MRI is at least as high as that of CT. Most adults with new-onset seizures should receive either a brain MRI or a head CT to exclude underlying symptomatic brain pathology. The utility of routinely checking serum glucose, electrolytes, and blood counts in adults with a first apparent unprovoked seizure in unknown but such checks are generally recommended.

Lumbar puncture (LP) is recommended for patients who are febrile or are otherwise suspected of having CNS infection. There is insufficient evidence to support the routine use of LP in adults presenting with a first apparently unprovoked seizure.

The CAVE score can predict the likelihood of late seizures after intracerebral hemorrhage. Key predictors were Cortical involvement, Age <65 years, Volume >10 ml and Early seizures within 7 days of ICH. The likelihood of late seizures was 0.6%, 4%, 10%, 35% and 46% for patients with 0 to 4 points.
The Status Epilepticus Severity Score has been prospectively validated (AUROCC 0.75) for the prediction of mortality in patients with status epilepticus.

A study identified 376 patients with a chief complaint of seizure; they were excluded if this was their first seizure, they had a ventriculoperitoneal shunt, or if they presented with focal neurologic deficits. Nine of ten patients with an abnormal head CT had a history of intracerebral hemorrhage, trauma, or active malignancy.
Diagnosis is made by clinical history or direct observation of a seizure; also consider movement disorders, sleep disorders, and psychogenic seizure.

Obtain an awake and asleep EEG; if epileptiform discharges are seen, proceed to treatment because, even after a single seizure, recurrence risk is substantially higher when EEG demonstrates epileptiform activity.

Strongly consider brain MRI (preferred) or head CT to exclude an underlying etiology. Baseline serum labs have low diagnostic yield but may help to ensure safety in initiating drug therapy. If seizures are atypical or a patient fails to respond to empiric antiepileptic drug therapy, admission for video-EEG monitoring should be considered.
See for initial therapy options for different seizure types. Consider felbamate, vigabatrin, ketogenic diet, and surgery for refractory seizures.
The decision to initiate antiepileptic medications after an initial unprovoked seizure should be individualized.B
Empiric antiepileptic drug monotherapy appropriate for seizure type () should be initiated after two or more unprovoked seizures occur on separate days. B

Most patients should start with an older medication such as phenytoin, valproate, or oxcarbazepine; alternative drugs effective for newly diagnosed epilepsy include lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, and topiramate. A

Failure of two or more empiric antiepileptic drug trials to produce seizure freedom constitutes refractory epilepsy; consider anterior temporal lobectomy for refractory mesial temporal lobe epilepsy. A
Sparse, low-level evidence exists for alternative and complementary medicine treatments and diets. B
The goals of epilepsy treatment are to produce seizure freedom without adverse medication effects. Provoked seizures do not usually require drug therapy.

Because recurrence risk is approximately 30% to 50% following one seizure, American Academy of Neurology guidelines (2015) suggest that observation without treatment for a single seizure is a reasonable option for selected patients.One would need to treat 5 five adults with a first unprovoked seizure for up to 2 years to prevent a subsequent seizure. Treatment can be considered when EEG demonstrates an epileptiform abnormality, when MRI demonstrates a corresponding symptomatic cortical lesion, or with nocturnal seizures because recurrence risk is higher in those settings.

Antiepileptic drug monotherapy should be initiated after two or more partial-onset seizures with either a standard medication such as phenytoin or alternatively with a newer drug such as lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, or topiramate. For primary generalized seizures, broad-spectrum drugs such as valproate, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, or topiramate are appropriate choices.

Monotherapy is favored by most experts, because it limits the potential for adverse effects and drug interactions. Drug dosing must be individualized to achieve optimal results. A second monotherapy should be tried if a patient fails to attain efficacy at an average to maximally tolerated drug dose or if the patient develops intolerable adverse effects. A randomized trial comparing initiation of standard vs new anti-epileptic drugs found that 44% of patients had an initial treatment failure, but 75% of these achieved 12-month remission at 6 years of follow-up. Those with more tonic-clonic seizures were more likely to fail.

There is no proved difference in efficacy between antiepileptic drugs, so choose a drug that provides a differing and complimentary mechanism of action or that offers potential efficacy for a comorbidity such as mood problems or migraine .For example, a systematic review found no evidence for different outcomes between carbamazepine and phenytoin as monotherapy or for immediate release compared with controlled release carbamazepine (although there was a trend for fewer adverse effects with the latter).

Any marketed antiepileptic drug can be used for adjunctive treatment. Topiramate, gabapentin, zonisamide, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, levetiracetam, clobazam, vigabatrin, and tiagabine, and pregabalin are somewhat effective as add-on treatments for patients with drug-resistant partial epilepsy.

For patients with generalized convulsive status epilepticus who continue to have seizures despite an appropriate dose of a benzodiazepine, IV phenytoin, fosphenytoin or valproate are recommended. Other options include levetiracetam, propofol, or barbiturates. A network meta-analysis identified phenobarbital as most likely to be effective as a second line drug in status epilepticus. However, the certainty of comparisons was mostly "very low".

A retrospective study of levetiracetam for benzodiazepine refractory status epilepticus in 218 patients found that the loading dose of levetiracetam (14.5 mg/kg, 28.8 mg/kg or 48.8 mg/kg) had no impact on rates of seizure termination at 60 minutes (93% low, 89% moderate, 85% high dose).
While felbamate has been recommended as add on therapy in drug resistant focal-onset epilepsy, a Cochrane review found 4 studies, with only 1 showing a benefit.

A Cochrane review that eslicarbazepine was effective as add-on therapy for adults with drug-resistant focal epilepsy (RR for 50% reduction in seizure frequency = 1.71, 95% CI 1.42-2.05) based on 5 studies with 1799 participants.

A systematic review identified 8 observational studies with 5637 patients comparing patients who did or did not receive seizure medication after mild or moderate traumatic brain injury. The studies consistently found a 0.6% absolute reduction in seizure frequency in the first 7 days after injury (95% CI 0.01% to 1.2%, NNT = 160). Levetiracetam, phenytoin and valproic acid were most frequently used. The authors caution that observational studies may overestimate benefit, and these drugs do have potential adverse effects.
A survey of trauma centers found that levetiracetam was the anti-seizure medication of choice, with a loading dose of 1000 mg followed by 500 mg twice daily as the usual dosing.
There is no evidence to support the use of calcium channel antagonists as adjunctive therapy for epilepsy.

A study identified 225 persons age 2 to 55 years with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome who experienced at least 2 drop seizures per week. They were randomized to cannabidiol 20 mg, cannabidiol 10 mg, or placebo. The median percent decrease in seizures was 42% in the 20 mg group, 37% in the 10 mg group, and only 17% in the placebo group. Adverse events were more common in the 20 mg group, making the 10 mg group the best balance between benefit and harm.
A systematic review of medical cannabinoids found moderate or high quality evidence for the use of cannabdiol for seizure disorder, with small to moderatre benefits (effect size 0.2 to 0.5).
Epilepsy surgery should be strongly considered when a patient develops refractory epilepsy. Complication rates have dropped dramatically over the past 30 years, based on a recent systematic review.

Surgical approaches may include resection of a symptomatic brain lesion, resection of a nonlesional epileptic focus, deep brain stimulation (DBS), brain-responsive neurostimulation or placement of a vagus nerve stimulator.

A systematic review identified 25 observational studies of surgical treatment for treatment resistant temporal lobe epilepsy, with 3031 patients undergoing temporal lobe resection and 288 undergoing magnetic resonance guided laser interstitial thermal therapy. Freedom from seizures occurred more often with resection (68% vs 57%) but any complications were more common with resection (14.6% vs 5.3%) but not major complications (2.1% vs 2.1%).
Anterior temporal lobectomy offers a 58% chance of seizure freedom postoperatively.
Vagus nerve stimulation reduces seizure frequency by half in 40% or more of implanted patients.
Sparse, low-level evidence exists for alternative and complementary medicine treatments in epilepsy, such as yoga, meditation, acupuncture, traditional Chinese medicine, cannabinoids, and vitamins.
There is no reliable evidence that relaxation, cognitive behavioral therapy, biofeedback, or educational intervention reduces seizure frequency.
Self-management education was shown in a systematic review of 13 randomized trials and 2 nonrandomized studies (overall high risk of bias) to improve knowledge and reduce seizure frequency.
Treatment of comorbid depression may require counseling or antidepressant medication.
Psychosocial counseling of the patient with epilepsy is important to address social limitations in driving and daily functioning in the home, school, and workplace.

Although there is some evidence from observational studies to support the use of ketogenic diets, data from RCTs are lacking. Ketogenic diets may be considered an option for motivated patients and/or families.

A network meta-analysis identified 12 RCTs with 907 patients comparing various dietary interventions (ketogenic, modified Atkins, and low glycemic index) for children with treatment resistant epilepsy. The authors conclude that the diet with the best evidence for efficacy and tolerability was the modified Atkins diet.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend intravenous immunoglobulins for reducing seizure frequency.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend yoga for reducing frequency of seizures.
Provoked seizures (see for causes) require no specific drug therapy other than supportive care and correcting or avoiding the precipitating factor.

Patients with acute repetitive seizures, prolonged seizures, or acute confusion from suspected nonconvulsive status epilepticus should be emergently triaged, then admitted for observation and emergent treatment with IV drugs if necessary.

A neurologist with special expertise in epilepsy should be consulted for assistance with diagnostic uncertainty, refractory epilepsy, or patients with intolerable adverse effects of treatment and those requiring complex polypharmacy regimens.
American College of Emergency Physicians guidelines state that physicians need not admit patients with a first unprovoked seizure who have returned to their clinical baseline in the ED.

Patients with epilepsy have an increased risk of psychotic symptoms, and anticonvulsants may precipitate psychosis in rare cases. A single small RCT found some improvement with olanzapine (n = 16 patients).
Most epilepsy is well-controlled by the first or second medication trial. B
One-third of epilepsy patients are refractory and require close and careful follow-up to avoid psychosocial limitations and physical injury from seizures. B
Approximately 60% of patients can eventually be successfully withdrawn from antiepileptic drugs. B

Only 33% of patients having a single unprovoked seizure have a second seizure within the next 2 years.Adolescents and adults 16 years or older with a single, unprovoked seizure who are seizure-free for at least 6 months have a less than 20% risk of recurrent seizure, regardless of treatment status.
However, the probability of a recurrent seizure is 49.5% in patients with epileptiform EEG abnormalities versus 27.4% in those with completely normal EEGs.
Sixty-five percent of those with two seizures have a third seizure.
Early antiepileptic drug treatment after the first or second seizure increases the probability of remaining seizure free for approximately 2 years but does not alter long-term outcomes.
Mortality is 40% during the 10 years following an episode of status epilepticus.
The risk of seizures following traumatic brain injury is 0.18% if mild, 0.41% if moderate, and 5.8% if severe.

Patients with post-stroke seizure have worse outcomes with higher mortality (OR 2.1, 95% 1.8 to 2.4), greater disability (SMD 0.6, 95% CI 0.4 to 0.8), and increased dementia risk (OR 3.1, 95% CI 1.3 to 7.7) than patients without seizure.
Sixty percent with newly diagnosed epilepsy achieve seizure freedom on the first or second medication.
Overall, more than 60% of persons with epilepsy enter remission for 5 years.

Patients who are seizure-free for longer than 2 years are candidates for withdrawal of antiepileptic drug therapy, although the optimal dosage-tapering regimen remains unclear. About 60% of those in remission can be successfully gradually withdrawn from antiepileptic drug therapy. These data are primarily from studies in children; studies in adults are lacking.

American Academy of Neurology guidelines (2021) updated their 1996 guidance regarding withdrawal of seizure medications. They recommend that adults who have been seizure-free for at least 24 months should engage in shared decision-making with their clinicians to determine the benefits and harms of continuing anticonvulsants. The panel could draw no conclusions as to the utility of EEGs or imaging in guiding these decisions among adults. The panel also could make no recommendations about medication withdrawal after epilepsy surgery.

One-third of patients develop refractory epilepsy; they are less than 5% likely to achieve seizure freedom with antiepileptic drugs. Frequent seizures at onset and symptomatic structural brain pathology are associated with refractory epilepsy.

In a long-term Finnish study of 245 persons with childhood epilepsy, persons who did not go into remission for at least 5 years had a 6-fold higher mortality risk than an age- and sex-adjusted comparison group.

The CAVE score can predict the likelihood of late seizures after intracerebral hemorrhage. Key predictors were Cortical involvement, Age <65 yars, Volume >10 ml and Early seizures within 7 days of ICH. The likelihood of late seizures was 0.6%, 4%, 10%, 35% and 46% for patients with 0 to 4 points.
Monitoring of therapeutic drug levels has not been well studied. In one RCT of 180 patients, monitoring drug levels did not improve outcomes during 1 year of follow-up.

Patients with well-controlled epilepsy should be seen at least annually to ensure adherence to, and tolerability of, AED therapy, to ascertain whether treatment may be withdrawn and to monitor for chronic complications of epilepsy and drug therapy.
Refractory epilepsy patients should be seen every few weeks or months to sequence antiepileptic therapies aggressively and to evaluate for nonpharmacologic treatment options such as surgery.

Routine adjustment of antiepileptic drug dosing to achieve particular serum levels is not advisable, but checking at least one baseline drug level once drugs have reached their expected steady state may still be helpful to ensure adherence and to assess possible drug interactions in polytherapy.
Patients should be educated to report medication adverse effects, to permit adjustment of therapy by the provider.
After one or more seizures, adults should be cautioned not to drive; check local jurisdiction for legal recommendations on seizure-free intervals.
Patients should also be instructed concerning other safety precautions, including avoidance of work at heights, operating dangerous machinery, and swimming or bathing without supervision.
Women of child-bearing potential should be counseled about risks of possible teratogenesis, drug interactions with hormonal contraceptives, and use of barrier contraception.
Family and caregivers should be counseled to recognize incipient status epilepticus (prolonged seizures lasting 5 minutes or longer) and when to call for emergency assistance.

Caregivers should also receive instruction on seizure first aid, including assistance to ground at ictal onset, moving dangerous objects and avoiding tongue or body restraint, and turning patient onto side in postictal period to avoid aspiration of oral secretions.

Older adults are more vulnerable to medication adverse effects and also more frequently have polypharmacy, raising risk for intolerability of antiepileptic drugs resulting from side effects and drug interactions.
Select antiepileptic drugs with a limited potential for drug-drug interactions.
If phenytoin is used, measurement of free drug levels may be helpful to avoid toxicity.

Most women with epilepsy have uncomplicated pregnancies. There is an increased risk of intrauterine growth retardation (3.8% vs 1.9%), antepartum hospital admission (42% vs 19%), and cesarean delivery (44% vs 33%).

A meta-analysis of 76 observational studies found that women with epilepsy have worse maternal and neonatal outcomes than women without epilepsy. This was true whether or not epilepsy was treated with an ASM. Taking an ASM was associated with worse neonatal outcomes than not taking. Polytherapy was associated with worse neonatal outcomes than monotherapy. The authors recommend co-management of these patients with an epilepsy specialist for counseling and medication optimization.

Planning for pregnancy should begin well in advance to determine whether AED therapy can be withdrawn or reduced from polytherapy to monotherapy. While preconception counseling is routinely recommended, it has not been well studied.
Maintaining antiepileptic drug monotherapy during pregnancy is reasonable in most instances; carbamazepine, phenytoin and phenobarbitone appear to be safe based on limited data.

Valproate use should probably be avoided during pregnancy if possible, given its higher rate of association with teratogenesis and cognitive impairment in the child, unless it is a specifically effective drug of choice for an individual patient.
This is confirmed by a study that found an increased risk of autism (HR 2.67, 95% CI 1.7 to 4.2) for valproate but not for topiramate or lamotrigine.

In a retrospective cohort study of more than 800,000 children in Denmark, there was no significant association between first trimester exposure to newer-generation drugs (eg, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine) and birth defects.
Women of child-bearing potential should receive folic acid daily.
Cognitively maldeveloped patients may be less able to report adverse drug effects and may have complex polytherapy regimens with other centrally active medications.
Drug level monitoring is an especially helpful adjunct in this population to avoid therapeutic overshoot and inadvertent toxic drug dosing.
A nationwide Danish study concluded that school performance is adversely affected by seizure disorder in children.

feature.caption: Properties of Antiepileptic Drugs.
feature.feature_body:
Drug Usual Total Daily Adult Dose (Intervals) Target Level (mcg/mL, or as Indicated) Adverse Effects Pharmacokinetic Issues Drug-Drug Interactions
Narrow-Spectrum Drugs
Absence of Seizures
Ethosuximide 500-1500 mg (bid) 40-100+ Aplastic anemia, hepatotoxicity, nausea, sedation None Unidirectional
Partial Seizures
Carbamazepine 400-1600 mg or higher (bid-qid) 4-12+ Aplastic anemia, ataxia, diplopia, dizziness, hepatotoxicity, hyponatremia, sedation Autoinduction, inducer Bidirectional
Gabapentin 900-3600 mg or higher (tid-qid) 4-20+ Dizziness, sedation, weight gain Limited absorption at high doses None
Lacosamide 200-600 mg (bid) Uncertain Dizziness, sedation None None
Oxcarbazepine 600-3600 mg or higher (bid) 10-40 (MHD) Dizziness, hyponatremia, sedation Mild inducer Bidirectional
Phenobarbital 90-180 mg or higher (qd) 15-40 Aplastic anemia, hepatotoxicity, psychomotor slowing, sedation Inducer Bidirectional
Phenytoin 200-400 mg (qd-bid) 8-20 Aplastic anemia, ataxia, dizziness, gingival hyperplasia, hepatotoxicity, neuropathy, sedation Inducer, zero-order kinetics. Bidirectional
Pregabalin 150-600 0.3-14 mg/L Dizziness, sedation, weight gain None None
Primidone 500-1500 mg (bid-tid) 5-12 Aplastic anemia, hepatotoxicity, psychomotor slowing, sedation Inducer Bidirectional
Tiagabine 16-64 mg (bid-tid) 100-300 mg/mL Dizziness, sedation, weight gain Inducible Unidirectional
Zonisamide 100-600 mg (qd-bid) 10-40 Dizziness, nephrolithiasis, paresthesias, weight loss Inducible Unidirectional
Broad-Spectrum Drugs (Partial Seizure and Generalized Seizures)
Felbamate 1800-4800 mg (bid-tid) 30-100 Aplastic anemia, hepatic failure, insomnia, irritability, weight loss Inducer Bidirectional
Levetiracetam 1000-3000 mg or higher (bid) 5-40+ Dizziness, sedation None None
Rufinamide 400-3200 mg/d Uncertain Sedation, diarrhea None Bidirectional
Topiramate 100-400 mg (qd-bid) 10-20 Cognitive complaints, nephrolithiasis, paresthesias, sedation, weight loss Inducer at doses >200 mg Bidirectional
Valproate 750-3000 mg (qd-tid) 50-100+ Aplastic anemia, hair loss, hepatotoxicity, nausea, pancreatitis, tremor, weight gain Heavily protein bound, inhibitor Bidirectional
Vigabatrin (for partial seizures and infantile spasms) 1000-4000 mg (bid) Uncertain Ataxia, headache, sedation, visual field deficits None None
Abbreviations: mcg/mL, micrograms/milliliter; nG/mL, nanograms/milliliter; mg/L, milligrams/liter; +, higher doses/levels may be effective, as tolerated; MHD, 10, 11; monohydroxyderivative, the active metabolite of oxcarbazepine; interactions, unidirectional indicates that other drugs may affect this AED; bidirectional indicates that other drugs may affect this drug and that this drug also affects other drugs; ?, based on premarketing data from clinical trials; Pk, pharmacokinetic issues; inducer, hepatic cytochrome P450 3A4 enzymatic inducer; inhibitor, hepatic cytochrome P450 2C19 enzymatic inhibitor; autoinduction, carbamazepine may increase its own metabolism, leading to a fall in serum levels and necessitating higher dosing, usually seen when first initiating carbamazepine; zero-order kinetics of phenytoin, saturable metabolism, in which smaller dose change may lead to greatly increased levels at higher dosing range, so dosage changes should be made cautiously and slowly, with blood level monitoring in selected patients.
